questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let $I = \int_0^{\pi/2} \dfrac{3\sin x + 4\cos x}{\sin x + \cos x}\, dx$

Using the definite integral property $\int_0^a f(x)\, dx = \int_0^a f(a-x)\, dx$, we get:

$I = \int_0^{\pi/2} \dfrac{3\sin(\pi/2 - x) + 4\cos(\pi/2 - x)}{\sin(\pi/2 - x) + \cos(\pi/2 - x)}\, dx$

$I = \int_0^{\pi/2} \dfrac{3\cos x + 4\sin x}{\cos x + \sin x}\, dx$

Adding the two equations for $I$:

$2I = \int_0^{\pi/2} \dfrac{3\sin x + 4\cos x + 3\cos x + 4\sin x}{\sin x + \cos x}\, dx$

$2I = \int_0^{\pi/2} \dfrac{7(\sin x + \cos x)}{\sin x + \cos x}\, dx$

$2I = \int_0^{\pi/2} 7\, dx$

$2I = 7[x]_0^{\pi/2} = \dfrac{7\pi}{2}$

$I = \dfrac{7\pi}{4}$

Answer: $\dfrac{7\pi}{4}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let $I = \displaystyle\int_{-\dfrac{\pi}{2}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} \sin^5 x \cos^7 x \ dx$

Let $f(x) = \sin^5 x \cos^7 x$

$f(-x) = \sin^5(-x) \cos^7(-x)$

$f(-x) = (-\sin x)^5 (\cos x)^7$

$f(-x) = -\sin^5 x \cos^7 x = -f(x)$

Since $f(x)$ is an odd function, the integral over the symmetric interval $[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}]$ is $0$.

$I = 0$

Answer: $0$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let $I = \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{dx}{e^x + e^{-x}}$.

Multiply the numerator and denominator by $e^x$:

$I = \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{e^x dx}{e^{2x} + 1}$.

Substitute $u = e^x$, so $du = e^x dx$. When $x=0$, $u=1$. When $x=1$, $u=e$.

$I = \int_{1}^{e} \dfrac{du}{u^2 + 1}$.

The integral of $\dfrac{1}{u^2 + 1}$ is $\tan^{-1}(u)$.

$I = [\tan^{-1}(u)]_{1}^{e} = \tan^{-1}(e) - \tan^{-1}(1)$.

Since $\tan^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$, we have $I = \tan^{-1}(e) - \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

Answer: $\tan ^{-1} e-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let $I = \int_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} \log \left( \dfrac{5 + 4 \sin x}{5 + 4 \cos x} \right) dx$.

Using the property $\int_{0}^{a} f(x) dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a - x) dx$, we have:

$I = \int_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} \log \left( \dfrac{5 + 4 \sin(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x)}{5 + 4 \cos(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x)} \right) dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} \log \left( \dfrac{5 + 4 \cos x}{5 + 4 \sin x} \right) dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} \log \left( \left( \dfrac{5 + 4 \sin x}{5 + 4 \cos x} \right)^{-1} \right) dx$

$I = - \int_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} \log \left( \dfrac{5 + 4 \sin x}{5 + 4 \cos x} \right) dx$

$I = -I$

$2I = 0 \Rightarrow I = 0$.

Answer: 0

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let $I = \int_{\dfrac{\pi}{6}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}} \dfrac{1}{1 + \sqrt{\tan x}} dx$.

Using the property $\int_a^{b} f(x) dx = \int_a^{b} f(a + b - x) dx$, we have $a + b = \dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

$I = \int_{\dfrac{\pi}{6}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}} \dfrac{1}{1 + \sqrt{\tan(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x)}} dx = \int_{\dfrac{\pi}{6}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}} \dfrac{1}{1 + \sqrt{\cot x}} dx$.

$I = \int_{\dfrac{\pi}{6}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}} \dfrac{1}{1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\tan x}}} dx = \int_{\dfrac{\pi}{6}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}} \dfrac{\sqrt{\tan x}}{\sqrt{\tan x} + 1} dx$.

Adding the two expressions for $I$:

$2I = \int_{\dfrac{\pi}{6}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}} \left( \dfrac{1}{1 + \sqrt{\tan x}} + \dfrac{\sqrt{\tan x}}{1 + \sqrt{\tan x}} \right) dx = \int_{\dfrac{\pi}{6}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}} 1 dx$.

$2I = [x]_{\dfrac{\pi}{6}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}} = \dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

$I = \dfrac{\pi}{12}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{12}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The integrand is $f(x) = \dfrac{|x-3|}{x-3}$.

Recall the definition of the absolute value function: $|x-3| = x-3$ if $x-3 > 0$ (i.e., $x > 3$) and $|x-3| = -(x-3)$ if $x-3 < 0$ (i.e., $x < 3$).

For the interval $[-2,2]$, we have $x < 3$ for all $x$ in the domain of integration.

Therefore, for all $x \in [-2,2]$, $|x-3| = -(x-3)$.

Substituting this into the integrand, we get $f(x) = \dfrac{-(x-3)}{x-3} = -1$.

The integral becomes $\int_{-2}^{2} (-1) dx$.

Evaluating the definite integral: $[-x]_{-2}^{2} = -(2) - (-(-2)) = -2 - 2 = -4$.

Answer: $-4$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let $I = \int_{0}^{1} x(1-x)^{99} dx$.

Using the property $\int_{0}^{a} f(x) dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a-x) dx$, we have:

$I = \int_{0}^{1} (1-x)(1-(1-x))^{99} dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{1} (1-x)x^{99} dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{1} (x^{99} - x^{100}) dx$

Evaluating the integral:

$I = \left[ \dfrac{x^{100}}{100} - \dfrac{x^{101}}{101} \right]_{0}^{1}$

$I = \dfrac{1}{100} - \dfrac{1}{101}$

$I = \dfrac{101 - 100}{100 \times 101}$

$I = \dfrac{1}{10100}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{10100}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: $\int_0^\pi \dfrac{e^{\cos x}}{e^{\cos x}+e^{-\cos x}} d x$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Let $I = \int_0^{\pi} \dfrac{e^{\cos x}}{e^{\cos x} + e^{-\cos x}} dx$.

Using the property $\int_0^a f(x) dx = \int_0^a f(a-x) dx$, we have:

$I = \int_0^{\pi} \dfrac{e^{\cos(\pi-x)}}{e^{\cos(\pi-x)} + e^{-\cos(\pi-x)}} dx$

Since $\cos(\pi-x) = -\cos x$, the integral becomes:

$I = \int_0^{\pi} \dfrac{e^{-\cos x}}{e^{-\cos x} + e^{\cos x}} dx$

Adding the two expressions for $I$:

$2I = \int_0^{\pi} \left( \dfrac{e^{\cos x}}{e^{\cos x} + e^{-\cos x}} + \dfrac{e^{-\cos x}}{e^{\cos x} + e^{-\cos x}} \right) dx$

$2I = \int_0^{\pi} \dfrac{e^{\cos x} + e^{-\cos x}}{e^{\cos x} + e^{-\cos x}} dx$

$2I = \int_0^{\pi} 1 dx = \pi$

$I = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let $I = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\cos x}{1 + \cos x + \sin x}dx$... (1)

Using $\displaystyle\int_0^a f(x)dx = \int_0^a f(a-x)dx$, substitute $x \to \dfrac{\pi}{2} - x$:

$I = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\sin x}{1 + \sin x + \cos x}dx$... (2)

Adding (1) and (2):

$2I = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\cos x + \sin x}{1 + \cos x + \sin x}dx = \int_0^{\pi/2} \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{1 + \cos x + \sin x}\right)dx$

$2I = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - J$ where $J = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \dfrac{1}{1 + \cos x + \sin x}dx$

Using half-angle: $\cos x = 2\cos^2\dfrac{x}{2} - 1$, $\sin x = 2\sin\dfrac{x}{2}\cos\dfrac{x}{2}$:

$J = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \dfrac{1}{2\cos^2\frac{x}{2} + 2\sin\frac{x}{2}\cos\frac{x}{2}}dx$

Dividing by $2\cos^2\dfrac{x}{2}$:

$J = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\frac{1}{2}\sec^2\frac{x}{2}}{1 + \tan\frac{x}{2}}dx$

Let $t = 1 + \tan\dfrac{x}{2}$, $dt = \dfrac{1}{2}\sec^2\dfrac{x}{2}dx$. Limits: $t: 1 \to 2$

$J = \displaystyle\int_1^2 \dfrac{1}{t}dt = \log 2$

$2I = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \log 2 \Rightarrow I = \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2}\log 2$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: $\int_\limits{-\dfrac{\pi}{2}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} \sqrt{\cos x-\cos ^3 x} d x \text{$ is equal to }
questions.solution:
The integral is $I = \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \sqrt{\cos x - \cos^3 x} dx$.

Since $\cos x - \cos^3 x = \cos x(1 - \cos^2 x) = \cos x \sin^2 x$, the integrand becomes $\sqrt{\cos x \sin^2 x} = |\sin x| \sqrt{\cos x}$.

The integral is $I = \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} |\sin x| \sqrt{\cos x} dx$.

Since the integrand $f(x) = |\sin x| \sqrt{\cos x}$ is an even function because $f(-x) = |\sin(-x)| \sqrt{\cos(-x)} = |-\sin x| \sqrt{\cos x} = |\sin x| \sqrt{\cos x} = f(x)$, we can write $I = 2 \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin x \sqrt{\cos x} dx$.

Let $u = \cos x$, then $du = -\sin x dx$. When $x = 0$, $u = 1$. When $x = \pi/2$, $u = 0$.

$I = 2 \int_{1}^{0} \sqrt{u} (-du) = 2 \int_{0}^{1} u^{1/2} du$.

$I = 2 \left[ \dfrac{u^{3/2}}{3/2} \right]_{0}^{1} = 2 \times \dfrac{2}{3} [u^{3/2}]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{4}{3} (1 - 0) = \dfrac{4}{3}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{4}{3}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $a$ is a real number such that $\int_\limits0^a x d x \leq a+4$ then
questions.solution:
The given integral is $\int_{0}^{a} x dx$.

Evaluating the definite integral:

$\left[ \dfrac{x^2}{2} \right]_{0}^{a} = \dfrac{a^2}{2} - 0 = \dfrac{a^2}{2}$

The given inequality is $\dfrac{a^2}{2} \leq a + 4$.

Multiplying by 2:

$a^2 \leq 2a + 8$

$a^2 - 2a - 8 \leq 0$

Factoring the quadratic expression:

$(a - 4)(a + 2) \leq 0$

The roots of the quadratic equation $a^2 - 2a - 8 = 0$ are $a = 4 and a = -2$.

For the inequality to hold, $a$ must lie between the roots, inclusive:

$-2 \leq a \leq 4$.

Answer: $-2 \leq a \leq 4$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: $\text{ If } I_n=\int_\limits0^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}} \tan ^n x d x \text{, for } n \geq 2 \text{, then } I_n+I_{n-2}=$
questions.solution:
Given $I_n = \int_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}} \tan^{n} x dx$.

Consider the sum $I_n + I_{n-2} = \int_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}} \tan^{n} x dx + \int_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}} \tan^{n-2} x dx$.

$I_n + I_{n-2} = \int_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}} \tan^{n-2} x (\tan^{2} x + 1) dx$.

Using the identity $\tan^{2} x + 1 = \sec^{2} x$, we have:

$I_n + I_{n-2} = \int_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}} \tan^{n-2} x \sec^{2} x dx$.

Let $u = \tan x$, then $du = \sec^{2} x dx$.

When $x = 0$, $u = 0$. When $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$, $u = 1$.

$I_n + I_{n-2} = \int_{0}^{1} u^{n-2} du$.

$I_n + I_{n-2} = \left[ \dfrac{u^{n-1}}{n-1} \right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{1}{n-1}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{n-1}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: $\text{ The value of the integral } \int_\limits{\dfrac{1}{3}}^1 \dfrac{\left(x-x^3\right)^{\dfrac{1}{3}}}{x^4} d x \text{$ is }
questions.solution:
Let $I = \int_{\dfrac{1}{3}}^{1} \dfrac{(x-x^3)^{\dfrac{1}{3}}}{x^4} dx$.

Factor out $x^3$ from the term inside the cube root:

$I = \int_{\dfrac{1}{3}}^{1} \dfrac{(x^3(x^{-2}-1))^{\dfrac{1}{3}}}{x^4} dx = \int_{\dfrac{1}{3}}^{1} \dfrac{x(x^{-2}-1)^{\dfrac{1}{3}}}{x^4} dx = \int_{\dfrac{1}{3}}^{1} \dfrac{(x^{-2}-1)^{\dfrac{1}{3}}}{x^3} dx$.

Let $u = x^{-2} - 1$. Then $du = -2x^{-3} dx$, which implies $x^{-3} dx = -\dfrac{1}{2} du$.

Change the limits of integration:

When $x = \dfrac{1}{3}$, $u = (\dfrac{1}{3})^{-2} - 1 = 9 - 1 = 8$.

When $x = 1$, $u = 1^{-2} - 1 = 0$.

Substituting these into the integral:

$I = \int_{8}^{0} u^{\dfrac{1}{3}} (-\dfrac{1}{2}) du = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{8} u^{\dfrac{1}{3}} du$.

Evaluating the integral:

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} [\dfrac{u^{\dfrac{4}{3}}}{\dfrac{4}{3}}]_{0}^{8} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{3}{4} [u^{\dfrac{4}{3}}]_{0}^{8} = \dfrac{3}{8} (8^{\dfrac{4}{3}} - 0) = \dfrac{3}{8} \times (2^3)^{\dfrac{4}{3}} = \dfrac{3}{8} \times 2^4 = \dfrac{3}{8} \times 16 = 3 \times 2 = 6$.

Answer: 6

questions.solution: Let $f(x) = \tan^{-1}  \left( \dfrac{1}{x} \right). The integral is \int_{-1}^{1} f'(x) dx$.The function $f(x)$ is discontinuous at $x = 0$. Therefore, the integral must be evaluated as the sum of two improper integrals:$\int_{-1}^{0} f'(x) dx + \int_{0}^{1} f'(x) dx = \lim_{t \to 0^{-}} [f(t) - f(-1)] + \lim_{t \to 0^{+}} [f(1) - f(t)]$.We know that $\lim_{t \to 0^{-}} \tan^{-1} \left( \dfrac{1}{t} \right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{2} and \lim_{t \to 0^{+}} \tan^{-1} \left( \dfrac{1}{t} \right) = \dfrac{\pi}{2}.Also, $ f(-1) = $\tan^{-1}$(-1) = -$\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $f(1) = \tan^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$Substituting these values:$\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2} -$(-$\dfrac{\pi}{4}$) \right) +$ \left( \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right) = \left( -\dfrac{\pi}{2} + \dfrac{\pi}{4} \right) + \left( \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{\pi}{4} =$-$\dfrac{\pi}{2} .$Answer:  -$\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: $\int_{-\pi / 2}^{\pi / 2} \sin ^2 x d x$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Let $f(x)=\sin ^2 x$
Now,
$\begin{aligned}
f(-x) & =\sin ^2(-x)=(\sin (-x))^2 \\
& =(-\sin x)^2=\sin ^2 x=f(x)
\end{aligned}$
So, $f$ is an even function
$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \int_{-\pi / 2}^{\pi / 2} \sin ^2 x=2 \int_0^{\pi / 2} \sin ^2 x d x \\
& \quad\left[\because \int_{-a}^a f(x) d x=2 \int_0^a f(x) d x, \text{ if } f \text{ is even }\right] \\
& =2 \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{1-\cos 2 x}{2} d x=\left[x-\frac{\sin 2 x}{2}\right]_0^{\pi / 2} \\
& =\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\sin 2 \times \pi / 2}{2}\right)-\left(0-\frac{\sin (2 \times 0)}{2}\right)
\end{aligned}=\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-0\right)-(0-0)=\frac{\pi}{2}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: $\int_0^2\left|x^2+2 x-3\right| d x \text{$ is equal to }
questions.solution:
Let $f(x) = x^2 + 2x - 3$. We factorize the quadratic expression as $f(x) = (x+3)(x-1)$.

The roots of $f(x) = 0$ are $x = -3 and x = 1$. In the interval $[0, 2]$, the function $f(x)$ changes sign at $x = 1$.

For $0 \le x \lt 1$, $x^2 + 2x - 3 \lt 0$, so $|x^2 + 2x - 3| = -(x^2 + 2x - 3) = -x^2 - 2x + 3$.

For $1 \le x \le 2$, $x^2 + 2x - 3 \ge 0$, so $|x^2 + 2x - 3| = x^2 + 2x - 3$.

The integral becomes $\int_0^1 (-x^2 - 2x + 3) dx + \int_1^2 (x^2 + 2x - 3) dx$.

Evaluating the first integral: $\left[ -\dfrac{x^3}{3} - x^2 + 3x \right]_0^1 = -\dfrac{1}{3} - 1 + 3 = 2 - \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{5}{3}$.

Evaluating the second integral: $\left[ \dfrac{x^3}{3} + x^2 - 3x \right]_1^2 = \left( \dfrac{8}{3} + 4 - 6 \right) - \left( \dfrac{1}{3} + 1 - 3 \right) = \left( \dfrac{8}{3} - 2 \right) - \left( \dfrac{1}{3} - 2 \right) = \dfrac{8}{3} - \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{7}{3}$.

Summing the results: $\dfrac{5}{3} + \dfrac{7}{3} = \dfrac{12}{3} = 4$.

Answer: 4

questions.q: $\int\limits_{-\pi / 2}^{\pi / 2} \sin ^2 x d x$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Let $I = \int_{-\pi / 2}^{\pi / 2} \sin^2 x dx$.

Since $f(x) = \sin^2 x$ is an even function, $f(-x) = \sin^2(-x) = (-\sin x)^2 = \sin^2 x = f(x)$.

Therefore, $I = 2 \int_{0}^{\pi / 2} \sin^2 x dx$.

Using the identity $\sin^2 x = \dfrac{1 - \cos(2x)}{2}$, we have $I = 2 \int_{0}^{\pi / 2} \dfrac{1 - \cos(2x)}{2} dx$.

$I = \int_{0}^{\pi / 2} (1 - \cos(2x)) dx$.

$I = [x - \dfrac{\sin(2x)}{2}]_{0}^{\pi / 2}$.

$I = (\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\sin(\pi)}{2}) - (0 - \dfrac{\sin(0)}{2})$.

$I = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - 0 - 0 + 0 = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

questions.solution:
The integral is $I = \int_{-\dfrac{\pi}{2}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} \cos x \, dx$.

The antiderivative of $\cos x$ is $\sin x$.

Applying the fundamental theorem of calculus:

$I = [\sin x]_{-\dfrac{\pi}{2}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}$

$I = \sin \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) - \sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)

Since \$sin $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) =1$ and $\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) =-1$, we have:

$I = 1 - (-1) = 1 + 1 = 2$.

Answer: 2$

questions.solution:
Let $I = \int_{-\pi / 2}^{\pi / 2} \sin x \, dx$.

The integrand $f(x) = \sin x$ is an odd function because $f(-x) = \sin(-x) = -\sin x = -f(x)$.

For any odd function $f(x)$ integrated over a symmetric interval $[-a, a]$, the integral is zero:

$\int_{-a}^{a} f(x) \, dx = 0$.

Therefore, $\int_{-\pi / 2}^{\pi / 2} \sin x \, dx = 0$.

Answer: 0

questions.q: If $I_{1}=\int_{0}^{\pi / 2} x \sin x d x$ and $I_{2}=\int_{0}^{\pi / 2} x \cos x d x$, then which one of the following is true?
questions.solution:
$I_{1}-\int_{0}^{\pi / 2} x \sin x d x=\left[-x \cos x+\int \cos x\right]_{0}^{\pi / 2}=[-x \cos x+\sin x]_{0}^{\pi / 2}=0+\sin \frac{\pi}{2}-0=1$
Similarly, $I_{2}=\int_{0}^{\pi / 2} x \cos x d x\quad=\left[x \sin x-\int_{\sin x]_{0}^{\pi / 2}}\right.\quad=[x \sin x+\cos x]_{0}^{\pi / 2}\quad=\frac{\pi}{2} \sin \frac{\pi}{2}-1=\frac{\pi}{2}-1$ Hence, $I_{1}+I_{2}=1+\frac{\pi}{2}-1=\frac{\pi}{2}$

questions.q: If $f(x)$ is defined in $[-2,2]$ by $f(x)=4 x^{2}-3 x+1$ and $g(x)=\frac{f(-x)-f(x)}{\left(x^{2}+3\right)}$, then $\int_{-2}^{2} g(x) d x=$
questions.solution:
Given that, $f(x)=4 x^{2}-3 x+1g(x)=\frac{f(-x)-f(x)}{x^{2}+3}$
Therefore,
$g(x)=\frac{\left(4 x^{2}+3 x+1\right)-\left(4 x^{2}-3 x+1\right)}{x^{2}+3}=\frac{6 x}{x^{2}+3}$
Now, $g(-x)=-\frac{6 x}{x^{2}+3}=g(x)$ which is an odd function. Thus, $\int_{-2}^{2} g(x) d x=0$

questions.q: If $\int_{\log 2}^{x} \frac{d y}{\sqrt{e^{y}-1}}=\frac{\pi}{6}$, then $x$ is equal to
questions.solution:
We have,
$\int_{\log 2}^{x} \frac{1}{\sqrt{e^{y}-1}} d y=\frac{\pi}{6}$
Let $\quad \sqrt{e^{y}-1}=t\Rightarrow \quad e^{y}-1=t^{2}\Rightarrow \quad e^{y}=1+t^{2}\Rightarrow \quad e^{y} d y=2 t d t\Rightarrow \quad\left(1+t^{2}\right) d y=2 t d t\Rightarrow \quad d y=\frac{2 t}{\left(1+t^{2}\right)} d t$
Now, $\int_{1}^{\sqrt{e^{x-1}}} \frac{2 t}{\left(1+t^{2}\right) \times t} d t=\frac{\pi}{6}\begin{array}{lc}\Rightarrow & \int_{1}^{\sqrt{e^{x}-1}} \frac{d t}{1+t^{2}}=\frac{\pi}{12} \\ \Rightarrow & \quad\left[\tan ^{-1} t\right]_{1}^{\sqrt{e^{x}-1}}=\frac{\pi}{12} \\ \Rightarrow \quad & \quad \tan ^{-1} \sqrt{e^{x}-1}-\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{12} \\ \Rightarrow & \quad \tan ^{-1} \sqrt{e^{x}-1}=\frac{\pi}{3} \\ \Rightarrow & \tan \left(\tan ^{-1} \sqrt{e^{x}-1}\right)=\tan \left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ \Rightarrow & \quad e^{x}-1=3 \Rightarrow e^{x}=4 \\ \Rightarrow & \quad x=\log 4\end{array}$
